I never played the original RE2 or RE3 back in the day, only the first one. With the remakes out, I figured “why bother,” but after spending some time with this, I was wrong.

Are the controls great? Not really. Tank controls definitely feel dated and take a little getting used to, but after about 10 minutes it starts to click and you’re moving around just fine.

What surprised me most is how well the game still holds up. The pre-rendered backgrounds have a ton of charm, and the tension is real. They packed even more zombies into this one, and walking into a room full of them still gets your heart going.

One thing I do miss in the newer games is the puzzles. The originals feel a bit more involved. Nothing crazy difficult, but they make you think just a little more.

On Steam Deck, performance is perfect now if you use Proton Experimental with the registry fix. It used to not boot at all, but that issue seems fully resolved.

If you’re an RE fan and have been on the fence about the originals, I’d say give them a shot. It’s a very different kind of survival horror, and still a great time.

Still a classic, albeit not a huge masterpiece. 

Some context: unlike nearly the entire rest of the series, I haven't played classic 2 or classic 3 since around the same time I first picked up Resident Evil 1 Remake, well over twenty years ago. And since it's been a few years since I played the 2019/2020 remakes, I figured I'd try the old versions again.

That wave of nostalgia hit and it really is still a wonderful game. I will say that if you're trying this for the first time, do it on Easy - these are TANK tank controls, and will definitely take 20-30 minutes to get used to. But once you're in, it's a very charming puzzle-based survival horror game.

Positives: The game isn't at all hard to understand or get into, it's never really boring, and you don't stay in one area for too long, unlike some of the other RE games. The licker scene especially is still iconic, just very chilling.

Negatives: ♥♥♥♥ the fights with G Birkin and the Super Tyrant in particular, plus those little G-spawn and roaches. You know the drill.

Also, and this might be a little bit controversial...the game just isn't scary? I was a little underwhelmed because I remembered this game being terrifying in my childhood, but then again, I was five years old. But I don't think I had any real fear or nerves the entire playthrough. The raw material that would later be perfected as the 2019 remake is definitely still there, but I guess this standard of horror really stopped working on me ages ago.

More negatives: each given run is actually quite short, which doesn't really make it better that getting a complete story out of it requires playing the same game FOUR freakin' times. That's an evil abuse of my time, even for 1998. The remake somehow making the runs way longer yet still not fixing this issue is even more evil, but that's for later.

More positives: Despite you basically knowing the full canon story by the time you finish Leon B, Claire B still offers some unique spooks and features, such as a confrontation with Mr. X on the RPD balcony and Chief Irons meeting an even more grisly end than before. So it's not ALL bone-dry repetition. 

Overall, a fun game and still worthwhile, but obviously dated and remade to perfection since.

This game is one of my favorites of all time and the Steam release brought back the same rush and feeling of nostalgia while looking great doing it. You play as both Leon and Claire in their own seperate scenarios in Raccoon City, solving puzzles, managing scarce equipment and small inventory space, while slowly uncovering the secrets of a viral outbreak. Its still impressive how the two different storylines intertwine and how decisions you make in scenario A changes your scenario B, making replayabilty very high, something not even the 2019 remake could emulate properly. 

The Steam version cleans up visuals and runs well while keeping the classic fixed-camera, tank-control, and vibe that might feel clunky (at first) to a modern audience but it also makes everything more tense and atmospheric. The story is still creepy, tense, and clever. The 2019 remake is slicker and more modern (over-the-shoulder camera, smoother combat), but it’s a different experience — the original’s charm and dread are its own thing. If you love classic survival horror or have nostalgia for this game, this Steam (or GOG) release is a must-play.

The OG Resident Evil 2 is a certified classic... but it hasn't aged quite as well as I expected it to. Over the past week I played and completed both the Claire (A) and Leon (B) scenarios on Normal difficulty. The playthrough with Claire felt more like Easy difficulty - I had a ton of first aid sprays and green herbs in my stash by the end of the game. Leon's scenario felt more challenging, mostly because of the final segment of the game and a couple battles. The scenarios are very similar, probably like 80%+ the same. Honestly, it kind of felt like an artificial way to make the game longer. I didn't use any guides, never looked anything up, and Claire's scenario took me longest at around 7 hours... and half of that time was spent running around in the police station looking for the right place to go. The police station is like a huge puzzle box... whereas the areas of the game that come after the police station mostly feel linear and easy to figure out. The tank controls - while it feels easier to manage in this PC port, it's still awkward and can screw you over in battles, especially when coupled with the three directional vertical aiming - lickers in particular are a pain mostly because of these awkward controls. Mr. X is not really a threat at all for most of this game... you can just run right by him and he won't follow you into the next room... they did a way better job with Mr. X in the remake. Also, this is probably just because the OG RE2 is 28 years old now, but I did not find it scary at all, whereas the remake genuinely got under my skin a few times. These issues aside, I still had a great time playing through the OG Resident Evil 2. It was my first time playing through it since the late 90's when my friend had it on his PlayStation... and I'm pretty sure we did *not* beat the game back then. I've played through the remake/remaster a few times and can tell you unequivocally that the remake is superior in almost every way, except for the atmosphere/vibes. Late 90's/early 2000's games have amazing atmosphere (Deus Ex is another great example of this) and Resident Evil 2 is no exception. If you don't have nostalgia for this OG version of Resident Evil 2, I can't think of many reasons to play it over the remake, especially since the remake is often on sale for $10 to $20 and this OG version costs $9.99. This is still a classic, but unless you want it for the nostalgia, to continue your RE collection or experience the early days of this amazing franchise... buying the remake instead is recommended. In 1998 I would have rated this game a 9.5 out of 10, but aging hasn't been as kind to it as expected, so in 2026 I rate it an 8.5 out of 10.

Resident Evil 2 is one of those rare games that truly ages like fine wine. Even decades after its original 1998 release, it still stands as a gold standard for the survival horror genre.

The level design alone is textbook material. Every area—especially the R.P.D.—is carefully crafted to balance tension, exploration, and efficiency. The game embraces backtracking as a core mechanic, but instead of feeling repetitive, it becomes deeply satisfying thanks to smart shortcuts and interconnected layouts. Combined with well-placed puzzles, returning to previous areas always feels meaningful rather than tedious.

What really elevates RE2 is its pacing. The game constantly shifts between moments of tension and brief relief, and it does so brilliantly by alternating between characters. But the true standout—the game’s defining feature—is the “Zapping System.”

This system does more than just offer two perspectives. Your actions in the A scenario directly influence the B scenario. Items you pick up, paths you unlock, even certain decisions you make can carry over and reshape the experience in the second playthrough. It creates a layered sense of progression where the world feels persistent and interconnected across both characters.

Because of this, the level design gains an extra layer of complexity. It’s no longer just about navigating spaces efficiently—it’s about understanding how your actions ripple across parallel narratives. And interestingly, even though you’re technically playing alone, you rarely feel alone. There’s a subtle but powerful illusion that the other character is out there somewhere, moving through the same world at the same time, dealing with their own challenges. That shared timeline gives the game a sense of presence and cohesion that very few games manage to achieve.

Another aspect that deserves more credit is the music. RE2’s soundtrack does an incredible job supporting the atmosphere—subtle, eerie, and never overbearing during exploration, but tense when it needs to be. And then there are the safe rooms: stepping into one feels like a breath of fresh air. The calm, almost soothing music creates a stark contrast to the danger outside, making those moments of safety feel genuinely earned and memorable.

Beyond the main campaign, RE2 also offers additional modes like Extreme Battle and The 4th Survivor, which add even more challenge and variety for players looking to push their skills further.

Looking back at 1998, Resident Evil 2 wasn’t just a great game—it was a phenomenon. And even now, it remains a masterclass in how to design survival horror the right way.

RE2 could be the greatest survival horror game ever made. I thought the first game was quite good for what it was, but EVERY aspect is improved in 2 to an extreme level. More unique weapons, much better looking models and pre-rendered backgrounds, and the story is phenomenal. This is a much darker version of the story that would be told in the remake, there were some truly jaw-dropping moments that I wont spoil here. RE2 is awesome. Although, the graphics, sounds and gameplay are almost identical to the original, RE2 still somehow finds a way to improve. The story is much more compelling then the original RE, and the characters are presented in a much more interesting way, making them more memorable and likable. The levels in RE2 are simply iconic too. Very well designed, very atmospheric and a blast to play around with. The puzzles are simple, but still very enjoyable to solve. The only major issue I have with RE2 (and the Remake for that matter) is the scenarios system. Instead of having two story paths leading to four different campaigns, which often contradict each other, I would have much preferred to have one story path leading to two, more thought out and well crafted campaigns. I don't mind that decision on its own, as it would certainly help with replayability. But it can lead to some head scratching in the later RE games, when someone references an event from RE2 that you've never seen because you accidentally played the non-canon path. If they made it obvious that Claire A - Leon B was the canon path, and Leon A - Claire B the non-canon, alternative universe path, then I wouldn't have an issue with this at all. But there is no way to know which path is canon, untill you play RE6. In case you're planning to play through the franchise for the first time, let me save you the headache and tell you that Claire A - Leon B is the canon path. Regardless, RE2 is still a phenomenal game, and honestly I enjoyed it more then the Remake. However, I would recommend playing both versions, as they are fundamentally different games and offer very different experiences.

Resident Evil 2 is such an awesome sequel, I was hooked until the very end.

I wasn't at all familiar with this game's story, so I was curious how RE2 would feel compared to RE1's setting, given that the majority of that game took place in a single (albeit restricted) mansion. This game feels a bit less like uncovering a mystery, and more so like dealing with the aftermath- and going on an adventure. I initially found this game felt much more difficult than the first, but after getting some proper ammo and managing to clear out the zombie infestation, the rest of the game was smooth-sailing. Not a cakewalk, but, the initial impression may make you think the difficulty leap compared to the first is a lot bigger than it actually is.

Saves this time are finite too - you can only save at a typewriter, provided you have have an ink ribbon (RE1 has infinite saves during your first Jill playthrough only, supposedly). It's a consumable, and so you can't really save scum. Not being able to save too frequently may add to the tension for some, but I found that this game never unfairly killed me in a way that cost me any real progress. There's more than enough ink ribbons for you to finish the story comfortably, so although it's a bit of a currency, it's not really something you need to worry about.

Being a blind playthrough w/ no walkthrough, it took me about 7.6 hours to finish this game (Leon A Story), but there's more to see. I'd only gotten "stuck" once, and it was pretty brief.

The only issue I had was that the game crashed once; I played on Steam Deck but I'm not sure I feel comfortable blaming SteamOS / proton.

I also wouldn't say it's [i]mandatory[/i] to play RE1 before this, but, you'd be robbing yourself of some semi-significant context.

Anyway, yes! I'd absolutely recommend checking out RE2 if you enjoyed the first game, or are favorable towards older games and love survival horror w/ environmental puzzles!

Okay, I'll admit that I was introduced to this series through the remakes, so I'm going to review it through that lens. I was too young to play these on release, and even if I was "allowed", I don't think I could've navigated via tank controls then.

But! I'll say that these games are wonderful!

The RE2 remake is probably the best of all the remakes, yet I think that having The Tyrant, Mr. X, show up in the A Series runs is the wrong call. He's too intimidating/overpowering for an A run. The meta-game knowledge you get from a second playthough allows you to navigate his shenanigans [sic: giant fists]. I've played Claire A and I'm in the sewers on Leon B, and even though I think that the Mr. X sections were contained due to system limitations, it was still more enjoyable that I only have to interact with him in a B playthrough - like a reward! I love when games reward you for playing them more deeply than the average player.

Also, the linking between Series is simple, yet effective. I upgrade inventory slots on Claire because of her Grenade launcher, but now my steak too juicy on Leon because I have a machine gun and a magnum with a lot of ammo. I like that this game is okay with giving you too many bullets on powerful weapons - actually let's you use them without feeling like you're punishing yourself.

Not without flaws, namely the sound design (footsteps, bullet casings) and endgame music (oh we're just blasting an alarm for the rest of the game and there's a decent chunk left?), but despite that, and knowing where it sits on the timeline of all game development, I honestly wish that the Remake was more to form: no Mr. X in the A Series, no Orphanage section (gruelingly punishing for not understanding that you're actually hidden under a table with no cloth draped over it), and way more posters of babes scattered on the walls (we used to be a proper society).

💾Graphics - This game is very old, so the visuals will not hold up, especially on a bigger screen. Now I did use the RE Enhanced mod and that made the experience so much better, and gave the whole game a remastered look. To me, this is the way to play the game. The visuals are all redone and the cutscenes are enhanced as well. Here is the mod I used to give this game the true remastered look: https://www.moddb.com/mods/reenhance-re2. I will say comparing the visuals to the original Resident Evil 1, this game is a significant upgrade! The environments are really detailed and show amazing environmental storytelling. Seeing the Police Station in its damaged and chaotic state really gives you an image of urgency and desperation. I love the visuals in this game, especially with the RE Enhanced mod.

🎮Gameplay - Resident Evil 2 is a huge jump compared to Resident Evil 1. Many quality of life improvements, harder enemies, and multiple playthroughs really add up to the experience. Resident Evil 2 offers 4 different playthroughs. Leon A/B and Claire A/B. B scenario being the true ending, but unlocked once completing the A scenario. In terms of puzzles, this game is pretty easy compared to RE1, which is a plus for me. The overall gameplay is harder when it comes to the enemies, especially on hard mode. You do have a lot of ammo in this game compared to its predecessor, but playing on the hard mode does improve that issue a good bit. You also have a really unique mechanic called the Zapping System. I suck at explaning it, so I’ll just copy and paste it from someone who explains it much better than I could. Here's a description of the Zapping System and how your actions carry over:
[olist]
[*]What you do in Scenario A affects Scenario B.
[*]The Weapon Locker: In the RPD basement weapons locker, you will find a Submachine Gun and a Side Pack (inventory expansion). Do not take both in Scenario A! Leave one (or both) for the Scenario B character, as they will need the help against deadlier foes.
[*]Cordite / Shutter: Using the cordite to close the shutters in Scenario A will prevent zombies from breaking through those windows in Scenario B.
[/olist]
The game also offers 3 special game modes. The 4th survivor is basically finding the extract and escaping, but dealing with many dangerous threats along the way. Tofu is similar to 4th Survivor, but much harder. And the best one is Extreme battle mode. This mode gives you a handful of characters to play as, find the bombs and escape. Each character has their own loadout, and every encounter and ammo locations are completely randomized. This is the way to experience RE2, with tons of fun game modes and its fun story and added difficulty setting.

📜Story - Resident Evil 2 has a great story. Now is it deep? Not really! To be honest if you want a deeper story, play the remake as that does a fantastic job with it’s story section. For the original, I still enjoyed it; and for its time it was a true classic! You will come across some interesting characters along the way as you make your desperate escape out of Raccoon City. You will come across villains, bosses and obstacles along the way. Reading the memos around the RPD gives some insight of the chaos that was happening before your arrival which I also really enjoyed.

🕛Playtime - This game is actually pretty long! You have multiple difficulty settings, up to 4 playthrough and special game modes and content to unlock. I added up to 9 hours with just two of the playthroughs alone!

🎧Sound - The music in this game is incredible. Older Resident Evil games always have amazing soundtracks. The voice acting has seen a massive improvement compared to the first Resident Evil game. Also the enemies (especially the Lickers) sound terrifying! 

❗Bugs❗- I haven’t really encountered any bugs here. The game played pretty good and saw no issues on my end.

🔅Performance - Performance is good. You should have zero issues with playing this game, especially with how old it is! No stutters or crashes either.

I have no idea how many times I played this game. I have ran this on probably 4+ different platforms. Back in the late 90s when it came out on PS1. Later on PS2 again, following that on PSP and now on PC. There is certainly a nostalgic sentimentality involved when I think of this game, and not just the original trilogy (all of which are some of my favorites), but this game in particular. This was the first game I played in the series, or in general the genre. Even after over two and a half decades later I still love playing this as much as I did as a kid.

I can't really describe how this felt. I remember my very first time I shot the shotgun in Leon A scenario. I fired and a zombie was cut in half. My 11 year old self lost his ♥♥♥♥. The awe and joy, back then games weren't like this. This is even before I knew I could aim up to pop the dome. Not only can I recall the experience, I know exactly where I was, who I was with, what time of day it was etc etc. It was a defining moment in gaming experience in my life. Nostalgia factor? ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ check.

Anyway this is the original fixed camera survival horror. For those who are only familiar with the modern remakes, this was way different. You fought the controls as much as zombies fought you. Eventually you were the expert, but it wasn't easy or intuitive as over the shoulder third person shooting we are more familiar with now. Still even now when I play it, I hardly struggle.

This game (and as well as other RE/Dino Crisis games) ooze atmosphere an tension. The soundtrack, from the ambient sounds, to footsteps, to zombie moans to licker tick etc etc. It all feels so distinctive, it all feels like you are in this tense fight for your life scenario. Even when I play modern games in the same genre. It always comes back to this. To further my point when I play RE2R and RE9 I still use the old BGM. The safe room BGM, the RPD tunes, etc etc. They were phenomenal. It creates such a strong aesthetic impact you will rarely find nowdays.

Game itself it actually simple. You run around solving puzzles and occasionally putting  a cap in someone's ass. Game supplies you with plenty of hardware. You play as either Leon or Claire. Each having two scenarios A and B. Each being complimentary to the other. Some decisions you make in Leon A will impact Claire B and so forth. While in today's standards that is nothing to write home about, back then that was groundbreaking. Do I leave that SMG for Claire, or the side pack? Or both?

Game primarily can be summed into proper route and inventory management. In itself the game is not difficult, and looking back on it, that was the correct thing to do. Gaming back then was still in it's infancy. Majority of us were kids. No way I'd be playing no damage SSS DMD runs back then...The game pretty much is strategically saturated with ammunition to kill everything that moves, while still managing to feel tense, suspenseful and enjoyable.  While in this time and age I played so many games with some insane audiovisual feedback for shooting.  Something like Cultic, Selaco, Doom Eternal on and on are just marvels, I still can't describe how my face lights up when I blast a zombie or few heads off with a shotgun. Or when I pull out the magnum and heads go boom. To this day, nearly three decades after, it is all so satisfying...

Story in all reality is silly. Especially considering how outdated the graphics are, no motion capturing, voice over being like someone's friend's had a drunken weekend recording so on and so forth. Yet still, Racoon City incident is iconic. I don't have to explain why. RE9 just came out and we still have not got past it. Racoon City incident is as iconic as Doom's Mars, FFVII's Midgar, Counter Strike's Dust II (yeah I went there, ♥♥♥♥ off) on and on. When I think of survival horror I think of Racoon City and Spencer Mansion. I Think of Leon, Claire, Chris and Jill. This game's impact is monumental, and if you can get past the outdated aesthetics. You will see why,

There is really not much to say here. I have been playing video games since I was maybe 5-6 years old. Back when Doom was out and it was all the rage. I lived through Build Engine games. Duke Nukem, Shadow Warrior, Blood, Tomb Raider, Fallout, Final Fantasy on and on, this is one of those giants. I don't say that lightly. There is a damn good reason so many of us point back to this (and RE3 Nemessis). This nearly three decades after it's inception, is still absolutely superlative.

Typically, when I go back and play the original verison of a game I played for the first time as it's remake, I typically can appreciate the game for it's time but still feel as if the remake is just vastly better. This is one of the first cases where I feel like the original was just as fun.

I liked Resident Evil 1 Remake, but the game was too annoying and difficult for me to really love it or have any desire to play it again anytime soon. Resident Evil 2 however is much more streamlined and easy to understand.The RPD is much easier to memorize and navigate compared to the Spencer Mansion, and the amazing soundtrack always kept you on your toes. There are much more resources compared to RE1R, but I felt like that helped out with this game as I always had enough Ink Ribbons to be able to enjoy the game instead of being worried I'll die to some thing and have to slog my way through the game again. I think part of it is that the game is much easier than RE1R, but I honestly prefered it that way. I was also shocked by how different the game was from the remake. The enemy placement was a lot different, and there was a lot more enemy variety. It made the game feel like a new experience even though I've played Resident Evil 2 Remake dozens of times. I can't say this game is better or worse than Remake, it's just different. And I like that because I was able to see how awesome this game was for it's time and how it really laid the foundation for Remake and the series going forward.

The story was also was pretty good. RE1R's story felt like a silly afterthought that really could have been an email, and although this game's story is no RDR2, for the time it was really impressive, and I was pleased with how it took itself seriously in a way that really enstilled the fear of environment and gameplay.

The only dissapointment I have to say about this game is the zapping system. For years, I have heard about amazing this system is, and how much better the A/B routes are in the original game over remake. They're better, but barely. I can only really think of one meaningful decision that impacts the B playthrough, at least what I noticed. It's mostly the same puzzles again, just like 2 remake. The story is more consistant than RE2R for sure, but you still end up doing the same puzzles Leon already did and it really makes no sense. I was expecting entirely new puzzles and enemy placement by how people described it, but it was really underwelming and overhyped. But I won't hold that against the game because I don't hold it against RE2R. I just see the B route as a slightly different way of replaying the game, and here it's the same thing.

I don't have major negative things to say about the game, and I never found it frustrating like RE1R. I can see myself replaying this many times, and I really liked it. I'm looking forward to Resident Evil 3: Nemesis now!!

An excellent game! So after playing through Resident Evil 3 Nemesis, I wanted to play the original RE2 as it’s such a legendary game. I am approaching this one differently to RE3 though, whereas with that game, I hated the remake but ended up loving the original, and with this one, I liked the remake, so I mainly was just interested to see what the original was like. So what did I think?

Like I’ve mentioned in the past, I love the PS1’s graphical aesthetic especially when it comes to horror games, and here it’s no different. The character models still look decent, especially for this being a late 90s game. Obviously the faces are static, but considering some of the other 90’s games I’ve played, this one stands out. Plus I did play with the HD mod, which makes everything look more smooth and like an actual remaster rather than just an updated GOG port.

The OST is of course incredible too with the save room music being so iconic and even some other tracks like the main hall RPD track. It also made me appreciate the sound design more, specifically since the game uses fixed camera angles and oftentimes the camera will be pointing in the opposite direction from where the enemies are coming from, so you have to rely on the sound to tell if you're doing damage to enemies and how close they are as you fire away.

As for the story, I’ll talk about both campaigns individually. I did a Claire A and Leon B route. Claire’s campaign, I remember liking more in the remake, since you have Sherry and Claire’s dynamic which is very endearing to watch, and it’s pretty sad when you see how ruthless and mostly non-caring her parents are. You encounter Annette Burkin in both campaigns but what I like about Claire's is that it shows the bit of the humanity that is still in her and that love she has for Sherry, whereas William seems to just care about his research. Also there’s the encounters with Chief Iron’s who I found to be a bit more comical in this version, especially when he’s threatening Claire with a pistol in the cutscenes, while she literally has a grenade launcher in her hands. Dude I can blow you up, BBQ you or melt you with Acid rounds, I win the who has the bigger gun contest lol Gameplay wise, I like Claire’s weapon line up, as her grenade launcher is just an awesome workhorse weapon to have with its multiple ammo types and good for crowd control. She also gets the crossbow, which is actually very effective at taking out zombies quickly, but it fires 3 bolts per shot, so you have to use it wisely.

Leon’s campaign I found to be good but less interesting overall. I found the running gag of him saying no one ever listens to him to be funny and his relationship with Ada is nice to watch grow. I did find his campaign more challenging overall, as I seemed to run into way more licker’s with him and they just eat shotgun rounds for breakfast. Plus you have Mr. X, who obviously is not the full on stalker like he is in the remake and basically was proto Nemesis, before RE3, but the few entrances he does have were pretty cool. Especially the one where you see him slowly walking towards the security camera. You can pretty much just run past and avoid him until the end when you do need to have a boss fight with him. Leon’s weapons are decent as I liked his pistol more, especially when you find an upgrade for it, and the shotgun is awesome with its upgrade. And the magnum is just great at clearing out rooms full of zombies. The flamethrower sucks hard though.

But ya, ya other than that the gameplay loop is still satisfying with the usual survival horror gameplay, though I did find the puzzles to be a little too easy compared to RE3, which had way more complicated ones.

Overall, a great game and I can see why fans of the series hold this one up there as one of the best. It does make me want to go back and replay the remake as I think I’d have a better love and appreciation for it now.

Back when I first started playing the Resident Evil franchise in 2023, I inevitably played Resident Evil 2 Remake. While it wasn’t the first Remake I played, having played Resident Evil 1 and 4 Remake beforehand, Resident Evil 2 Remake was the game that made me interested in playing the Original trilogy. This was during a time where I still had the mindset of “There’s no way the Originals can be better. The Remakes just improve on everything the Originals do, right?”, and while I’ll dive deeper into that topic in a future review, I will say that this is the RE game that proved that mindset wrong. Since then, I’ve played through RE2 more times than I can count. And now, with the Original trilogy finally released on Steam, AND on sale, I have another excuse to replay them. And I must say, RE2 is a game that never gets old.

Story:
RE is a franchise that I play purely for the gameplay, not the story. So when an RE game’s story is ♥♥♥♥ (which are most stories in the franchise), I don’t really let it weigh on my overall opinion on the game. But I must say, RE2 has a surprisingly decent story. Not anything groundbreaking or insanely good, but decent. Characters and their motives are consistent. Some even get development that isn’t half assed. Ada, who is a character I strongly dislike, is actually tolerable in her debut here. Likeable, even. It’s a shame subsequent entries ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ destroy any sense of morality and likeableness in her character. But anyways, I gotta give the story some props. Not half bad.

Resource & Inventory Management:
As a sequel, RE2 decided to go big or go home. And they most definitely did NOT go home. RE2 is bigger in a lot of ways, including enemy count, which has been significantly increased. As a result, the amount of ammo and healing spread across the game is increased, but not to the point where it feels like the entire game is on easy mode. There’s a good balance, so that you still need to think about how you’re using your ammo and what type of ammo you’re using for certain situations. Because things are more bombastic and high stakes, it makes getting through enemy encounters unscathed and successfully saving up stashes of ammo and healing even more satisfying than it was to do in the first game.

Enemy Selection:
There’s a lot of returning enemies as well as a couple new comers. Zombies are back, with some balancing changes to account for the sheer amount of zombies throughout the game. Dogs, crows, and spiders return but essentially the same as they were in RE1. Two new enemies appear: The Lickers and Ivies. Lickers function as a much more fair version of the Hunters from RE1, and their gimmick of being blind is really fun to exploit. Ivies show up in the Labs and are sort of like a puzzle enemy, the solution to their puzzle being fire. I’d call it a pretty good improvement over RE1’s selection.

Puzzles:
Sadly, puzzles haven’t exactly seen an improvement. They’re pretty much on par with RE1’s puzzles. A lot of “use this thing on that”, which isn’t exactly all that engaging. Sliding box puzzles are also back, but at least there’s less of them and they’re all a bit more brief.

Zapping System:
RE2 introduces the zapping system to gameplay. Specific choices the player makes and certain items the player picks up as their first character will have an effect on their second character. For instance, your first character can come across a weapons locker with two items in it. You could take both items, but that means your second character misses out on both of them, so it’s best to leave behind whichever item you think would be best for your second character. It adds another layer of strategy to the gameplay.

Locations:
I think it goes without saying that the RPD is one of, if not, the best, most iconic location in all of gaming. They somehow took something as intricately designed as the Mansion, and one upped it in just about every way, whether it be visually, or physically, with how rooms flow through the building and interconnect with other rooms to provide a location that’s very fun to route through and master. The RPD Parking Lot, Sewers, and Lab are weaker locations, but still a good time, and an improvement over the Guardhouse, Tunnels, and Lab from RE1.

The Four Scenarios:
RE2 offers a lot in the way of replayability, and that’s thanks to the four different scenarios available. Parts of the story, such as how people die or interact with each other, and your objectives can change significantly depending on which character you play as first. The enemies you fight and the items you can find will also change between all four scenarios, and the A and B story intersect at multiple points, with characters from both sides running into each other and interacting. Leon A, Leon B, Claire A, and Claire B are all different experiences that are worthy of a playthrough.

Bosses:
Bosses are also generally better than RE1’s bosses, focusing on the player’s mastery of tank controls and positioning, making bosses much more engaging. What also makes these bosses interesting is that none of them are exclusive to either character. It all depends on which character plays through the first story, and which character plays through the second. This allows players to use the appearances of bosses to string together a timeline of what Leon and Claire are simultaneously doing throughout their time in the RPD.

General Improvements:
There’s quite a bit of improvements that are seen through less significant changes, such as weapon balancing changes (primarily the grenade launcher). QoL improvements primarily come from changes and additions to the inventory like being able to stack items from the item box and being able to use healing items despite being at full health to make space. And, finally, character model and animation improvements. Models look a bit more detailed and clear, and the animations for characters are much less stiff, in most cases doing a better job at visually conveying actions the characters are doing.

Side Content:
There’s much more side content this time around. This game has the first instance of a ranking system in an RE game’s main story. It’s very fun to go for A rank and it requires a lot of planning and strategy that constantly pays off and feels great to achieve. You can unlock two extra modes; 4th Survivor and Tofu Survivor, which are both brutally challenging but fun tests on your mastery of resource management and movement. The secret costumes for RE1 also make a return.

OST:
The OST in this game was ahead of its time. The ambient tracks elevate the already great atmosphere and stick with you. Other tracks emulate sweeping orchestral music. Characters even have motifs. RE2’s OST goes down as some of the best OST in any video game ever despite it’s limitations, and the best OST in the entire franchise.

Final Verdict:
RE2 was a big step in the survival horror genre, and it had a lot of pressure to successfully take that step instead of falling flat on its face. But it didn’t just take a step. It took a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ leap and stuck the landing. RE2 is what I’d consider to be a perfect sequel. The stakes are heightened, there’s improvements all over the board, and there’s more content to partake in. It’s also just an amazing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game, and one of my favorite games ever, being the second best entry in the RE franchise (right behind Resident Evil 4 Remake), in my humble opinion. Don’t miss out on one of the best survival horror experiences ever.

It was the year 2000. I was eight years old and I was spending the day at my grandma's house. My Uncle had a PlayStation 1 and I noticed he was playing a game I've never seen before...It wasn't Super Mario 64, it wasn't Pokemon or anything else I was playing at the time. It was something I had never seen before. Suspenseful ambient music, no HUD, just a cop running through an alleyway killing zombies.

I asked him if I could play and he let me try it and I couldn't even for the life of me, I could not figure out how to aim. I was just thinking, like, 'Oh you just move and attack with just one button' but no, you needed two buttons. One to aim and one to shoot.

At this point, this game had really piqued my interest at such a young age. Every time I would visit my Grandma's house, I would ask my uncle if I could play this game. Just a little bit at a time; I didn't really play too much but it was enough to spark an interest in a series that I'd never heard of before.

It wasn't that long after the GameCube came out and RE2/RE3 and the RE Remake and RE0 came out. 

Out of all the games in the series at that time, it was Resident Evil 2 that had stood out to me from its gameplay, graphics, and story that had really made me dive deeper into the lore of Resident Evil.

From then on out, the rest was history: I started collecting the games and merchandise, playing them across various consoles, and really took an interest in the series as a whole. Heck, one of the only conspiracy theories I generally believe is that a zombie apocalypse is possible because of this series. Even recently at New York Comic-Con in 2025, I had my copy of Resident Evil 2 on GameCube autographed by Alyson Court, the voice actress of Claire Redfield, with the quote "What's going on in this town?" written across the cover.

Although this game has been on various consoles and since the GOG release has been much more accessible to people in a legitimate fashion, having this on Steam now gives it an even further reach into audiences that have been untapped. 

This game may not be the "magnum opus" of the Resident Evil series. That may be the Resident Evil remake on the GameCube. It may not be the most action-packed adventure like Resident Evil 4. To me, Resident Evil 2 1998 has been my all-time favorite video game and nothing has since changed that opinion of mine. I forever love the series and I will forever love this particular game.

..I hope those, whether new to the series or long-time veterans, enjoy this game as I have since I was 8 years old.

To me, the 1998 original of Resident Evil 2 is more than just a game; it is a tribute to the most remarkable character in the franchise: [b]Claire Redfield[/b]. While I enjoy the remake, only this version captures her true essence. 
[/quote]
[h2] Why She Is So Special [/h2]
As a man, I find Claire's character to be an incredible representation of what makes the other sex so uniquely powerful and admirable. It’s not just about her being "tough"—it’s about [i]how[/i] she is strong.
[list]
[*] [b]Love as a Mission:[/b] Her journey to find her brother Chris isn't just a plot point; it's born from a deep, selfless appreciation for her family. This level of empathy and dedication is something you rarely see highlighted, making her search feel incredibly human and noble.
[*] [b]Pure Character:[/b] Claire isn't a trained soldier; she’s a student with a leather jacket and a motorcycle. Her bravery feels earned because it comes from the heart, not from a tactical manual.
[*] [b]The Emotional Core:[/b] Her bond with Sherry Birkin in the 1998 version remains one of the most touching storylines in gaming history. She brings a level of compassion to the survival horror genre that is unmatched.
[*] [b]Grace Under Pressure:[/b] She faces the nightmare of Raccoon City with an unbreakable spirit, proving that kindness and strength can go hand in hand.
[/list]

Resident Evil 2, developed and published by CAPCOM Co., Ltd. and later made available on PC platforms like GOG.com, represents a defining moment in the evolution of survival horror—one where the genre’s core ideas were not only refined but expanded into something far more ambitious and cohesive. Set against the catastrophic downfall of Raccoon City, the game drops players into a world already consumed by infection, where the horror is not creeping in from the edges but has fully taken hold. This shift in context gives the experience an immediate sense of urgency, as every location feels like part of a larger, collapsing ecosystem rather than a contained incident.

A major strength of the game lies in its dual-protagonist structure, following Leon S. Kennedy and Claire Redfield through overlapping but distinct scenarios. This design does more than simply offer replay value—it builds a layered narrative that rewards curiosity and attention. Each character experiences different events, encounters unique allies, and approaches the same locations from varying perspectives, creating a sense of continuity that was rare at the time. The way these scenarios interlock gives the story a dynamic quality, making the player feel like they are witnessing multiple facets of a single disaster rather than replaying the same sequence with minor changes.

The gameplay itself refines the survival horror formula into a more polished and engaging loop. Resource management remains at the heart of the experience, with limited ammunition and healing items forcing players to think carefully about every encounter. Combat is deliberate rather than empowering; even basic enemies can be dangerous if approached recklessly. This tension is balanced by thoughtful level design, particularly within the Raccoon City Police Department, which serves as a sprawling hub filled with puzzles, shortcuts, and hidden connections. Navigating this space becomes a central part of the experience, as players gradually unlock new areas and piece together efficient routes through previously hostile territory.

Visually, the game pushed the capabilities of its time, using detailed pre-rendered backgrounds to create environments that feel both grounded and oppressive. The urban decay of Raccoon City is conveyed through subtle environmental storytelling—overturned vehicles, blood-stained corridors, and makeshift barricades all hint at the desperate attempts to contain the outbreak. Character models, while simple by modern standards, were expressive enough to convey personality and emotion, particularly in key story moments. Paired with a carefully crafted soundscape that blends ambient noise with sudden, jarring cues, the game maintains a constant sense of unease without relying excessively on cheap scares.

What truly elevates the experience is its pacing. The game alternates between moments of quiet exploration and bursts of intense danger with remarkable precision. Just as players begin to feel comfortable, the game introduces new threats or unexpected encounters that disrupt their sense of control. This ebb and flow keeps tension consistently high, ensuring that the player never fully relaxes. Decisions—whether to conserve ammunition, which paths to take, or how to manage inventory—carry lasting consequences, reinforcing the survival aspect at every turn.

The narrative, while rooted in familiar horror tropes, benefits from a stronger sense of character and emotional grounding than many of its contemporaries. Leon’s journey from inexperienced rookie to capable survivor and Claire’s determination to find her brother provide personal stakes that anchor the broader disaster. Supporting characters add further depth, contributing to a story that feels more cohesive and engaging than the series’ earlier efforts. Although some elements, such as voice acting and dialogue delivery, reflect the limitations of the era, the overall narrative remains effective due to its clarity and momentum.

Even when viewed through a modern lens, Resident Evil 2 (1998) retains a remarkable level of impact. Its mechanics may feel deliberate and occasionally rigid compared to contemporary standards, but these qualities are integral to its identity. The fixed camera angles, deliberate controls, and emphasis on planning over reflexes all contribute to a carefully constructed experience that prioritizes tension and atmosphere above all else. Rather than feeling outdated, these elements serve as a reminder of a design philosophy that values restraint and intentionality.

In the end, Resident Evil 2 stands as a cornerstone of survival horror, not simply because it improved upon its predecessor, but because it demonstrated how far the genre could evolve without losing its core identity. Its combination of layered storytelling, thoughtful design, and relentless tension creates an experience that remains compelling decades after its release. It is a game that understands exactly what it wants to be and executes that vision with confidence and precision, securing its place as one of the most important titles in gaming history.

Shoutout to Chedd for providing this fix for Dino Crisis 1 & 2 to make the game at least playable on Linux. This will work for RE as well. I am running Bazzite currently. 

****** LINUX / STEAMDECK FIX ******

You need PROTONTRICKS installed, you also need to set Resident Evil 2 compatibility mode to Proton 8 in the Steam properties.

So, try to run the game, the game will throw an error when a pop up comes up asking you to essentially register a .REG file.

Open Protontricks and then select the default prefix, open REGEDIT.

Back on Steam, right click Dino Crisis and get yourself to the installation folder.
Should look like: /home/chedd/.local/share/Steam/steamapps/common/xxx_Biohazard2

Now once here, right click the re2_(yourlanguage).reg file and copy it to your home folder, example: /home/chedd/


Now go back to the Protontricks REGEDIT.
Click on REGISTRY in the top left. "Import Registry File".
In the "Look in" box, select drive "/"

Open the home folder, "USERNAME" folder. Select the re2_(yourlanguage).reg file and press open.

Close it all down.

Go back to Steam and go into Resident Evil 2 properties and enter WINEDLLOVERRIDES="ddraw=n,b" %command% in the startup properties.

All should work.

****** SAVING ON LINUX/STEAMDECK FIX BELOW ******

Fix for saving in Linux below:

Edit the re2_{language}.reg reg key and replace the Windows path with the following path ".\\Saves"

Restart your game and you can now save. You can test this quickly by going to Special > Extra Battle > Stage 1 > Any Character > Run towards the top of your screen and there is a typewriter you can try to save on. If the game doesn't crash then you did it correctly :)

****** END OF TROUBLESHOOTING GUIDE ******

If you grew up with classic survival horror, Resident Evil 2 isn’t just a game it’s a core memory.

Coming back to RE2 (1998) feels like stepping into a time capsule where atmosphere mattered more than action, and every bullet counted. The fixed camera angles, pre-rendered backgrounds, and tank controls might seem dated to newcomers, but for OG players, that’s exactly where the magic lives. The tension, the uncertainty, the iconic sound design it all still hits.

Playing as Leon S. Kennedy in his rookie days is something special. There’s a charm to his character here less polished, more human that makes his journey through Raccoon City unforgettable. Watching him grow from a naive cop into someone who can survive the nightmare around him is part of why this game sticks with fans.

The police station remains one of the best-designed locations in gaming history equal parts puzzle box and death trap. Every hallway tells a story, every door feels like a risk. And let’s not forget the soundtrack subtle, eerie, and perfectly timed.

For longtime Resident Evil fans, RE2 (1998) is comfort horror at its finest. It’s not just nostalgia it genuinely holds up as a masterclass in pacing, atmosphere, and survival design.

This is where legends were made and where Leon became Leon.

Rating 10/10⭐

Open regedit 
Go to HKEY_USERS > S-1-5-21-[..] > Software > CAPCOM > STEAM_R EVIL2
Change the data of "Save Path" to C:\Saves\ from F:\Games\RE2\Save

Regarding the game itself - don't get me wrong, the title is great. The very beginnings of Leon Kennedy and Redfield Family, a rather intriguing story and a lot of replayability value both in the original version of the game and in Remake.

Regarding the port itself? Boy, it's a tricky question.

I already reviewed Resident Evil 3: Nemesis from the classical trilogy. Everything is as bad even here.

The release of the classic games is a great surprise, and I do think that it is a great way to get acquainted with them: you don't have to use emulators or search for a copy, you just pay $5.00 per game and you are good to go!
But is it actually a good choice considering everything which goes on underneath?

The good part - there is now a chance to experience the original RE2, with the original B scenarios which have way more differences than in the Remake.

The underwhelming part? All the same as in RE3:Nemesis.
- No achievement system
- No cloud saves
- The Enigma Protector DRM (WHY?)
- Pixelated image (no proper aspect ratios, no upscale, and I DO NOT mean AI nor RTX/DLSS as some might think).
- Very little options to tweak the game's settings (meaning all you can do is reassign controls and change the resolution)
- The game checks your registry and does some "corrections" in it. What for, and why doesn't RE3 have that as  well?

There is actually a launcher coming with the game, which is... you guessed it, useless, because seemingly the settings you apply don't even work accordingly.
